e.etymology: A respelling of Carrie, the pet form of Caroline, a feminine form of Charles, from Germanic karl, 'free man'.
A spelling of Kristin, the Scandinavian form of Christina, from Latin Christianus, 'follower of Christ'.
Coined by Henrik Ibsen for the Bedouin chief's daughter in his 1867 play Peer Gynt. Edvard Grieg's music for the play includes the well-known Anitra's Dance.
A feminine form of George with the -ene ending, used in the US in the mid-1900s. George comes from Greek georgos, 'farmer', literally 'earth worker'.
An elaboration of Myrtle used in the American South in the early 1900s, close to Myrtis. Myrtle is the evergreen shrub, from Greek myrtos.
A short form of Clement, from Latin clemens, 'merciful, gentle', the name of an early pope and saint. It is also short for Clementine.
An English surname from a place name built on Old English weard, 'watch', and hyll, 'hill'. NBA star Stephen Curry's first name is Wardell, after his father, Dell Curry.
A spelling that sits between Cherry, the fruit used as a name, and Cherie, from French chérie, 'darling'.
A respelling of Brittany, the English name of the region of northwest France settled by Britons in the 5th century. Brittany became a popular American girls' name in the 1980s.
A respelling of Cassandra, the Trojan princess of Greek myth whose true prophecies were never believed. The meaning of the Greek name Kassandra is uncertain.
A misspelling of Gerald found in US records. Gerald comes from Germanic ger, 'spear', and wald, 'rule', and was brought to England by the Normans.
Built from Gay or Gaynor and the -nell ending, as in Raynell and Darnell; used mostly in the American South in the 1930s and 40s.
A phonetic American spelling of Siobhan, the Irish form of Joan, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'. It also fit in with the Sha- names popular in the 1970s.
An English surname from places named with Old English mere, 'lake, pool', and tun, 'settlement'.
A spelling of Christa, a short form of Christina, from Latin Christianus, 'follower of Christ'.
An English surname from places called Melton, most of which mean 'middle settlement', from Old English middel reshaped by Norse speakers, plus tun.
A misspelling of Samantha that appears in US records from that name's peak years. Samantha was first used in 18th-century New England, probably as a feminine form of Samuel.
A spelling of Katina, a Greek short form of Katerina (Catherine). Katina jumped in the US in 1972 after a baby was given the name on the soap opera Where the Heart Is.
A transposed spelling of Stephanie that appears in US records from that name's peak years. Stephanie is the feminine of Stephen, from Greek stephanos, 'crown' or 'wreath'.
A Scottish pet form of Kirstin, the Scots form of Christina, from Latin Christianus, 'follower of Christ'.
A spelling used for both Cherry, the fruit name, and Sherri or Cherie, from French chérie, 'darling'.
A respelling of Kathleen, the English form of Irish Caitlín, which is the Irish form of Catherine. Catherine has long been tied to Greek katharos, 'pure'.
A phonetic spelling of Lisa, the short form of Elisabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, 'my God is an oath'.
A surname used as a first name, familiar from actors Henry, Jane and Peter Fonda. The family name came to New York with Dutch settlers in the 1600s. Fonda is also Spanish for an inn.

assoc.t: the Fonda acting family: Henry, Jane and Peter

e.etymology: A respelling of Cheryl or Sheryl, a 20th-century English coinage that probably blends Cherie or Cherry with the ending of Beryl.
A misspelling of Clarence found in US records. Clarence comes from the English royal title Duke of Clarence, created in 1362 and named for the town of Clare in Suffolk.
An American name of the 1800s, most likely Dora with the El- of Eleanora and Elnora. It also echoes Spanish el dorado, 'the golden one', the source of the town name Eldora in Colorado.
An African American name of the 1970s that puts the Ta- prefix on Wanda. Tawanda is separately a Shona name from Zimbabwe meaning 'we have become many'.
A respelling of Danielle, the French feminine of Daniel, from Hebrew Daniyyel, 'God is my judge'.
From the Old English name Ealdred, joining eald, 'old', and raed, 'counsel'. It survived as a surname and came back as a first name; actor Gregory Peck was born Eldred Gregory Peck.
